newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Emperor's grandson says ditch Austria neutrality.
newsitem.headline: Emperor's grandson says ditch Austria neutrality.

text.p: Karl Habsburg, grandson of the last ruler of the Austro-Hungarian empire, said on Friday Austria must ditch its neutrality and join NATO.

Habsburg, standing in European elections on Sunday on a conservative People's Party ticket, is almost assured a place among the 21 seats allocated to Austria in the Strasbourg-based European Parliament.

"There is no role for Austrian neutrality, in fact there hasn't been for the last 15 years," Habsburg told Reuters in an interview at the baroque Schoenbrunn Palace, his ancestors' former summer residence.
"I hope Austria will in the near future become an integral part of the Western European Union (WEU) and NATO," he said following the People's Party's last rally before the poll.
His comments in favour of scrapping neutrality were unusually forthright for a representative of the People's Party, which rules Austria in coalition with the Social Democrats.
The Social Democrats of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky oppose NATO membership but the People's Party says neutrality should be reviewed in the future.

Sitting in a coffee house overlooking the palace, where his family once ruled an empire stretching from the Adriatic to modern-day Ukraine, Habsburg said it felt natural to represent Austria in Europe.
"My family have been professional politicians for the past 800 years, so it feels absolutely natural," said Habsburg. He added that he was comfortable with Austria's republican constitution.
If elected the 35-year old professional pilot and former games show host will join his father Otto, who has been a German member of the European Parliament for 17 years.
Habsburg is number two on the list of the People's Party, which is likely to win around six seats in the Euro assembly.
Otto von Habsburg, spent his early childhood at Schoenbrunn before his father Kaiser Karl I was forced to abdicate in 1918, following Vienna's defeat in World War One.
Karl was born in Germany and only emigrated to Austria in 1968 after his father renounced his right to the throne.
He said he did not feel any nostalgia for his regal past although he was a strong supporter of monarchy.
"For the last 50 years all the monarchies in Europe have been first-class democracies, and that's definitely something you can't say about the republics in Europe," he said.
Karl, who is campaigning on a platform of tolerance and family values, stressed the family unit was all-important and said he was totally opposed to the idea of homosexual marriage.
"Family for me is father, mother and kids...Homosexuals should not get the same protection as families," he said.
Habsburg, who has worked to defend the rights of immigrants and ethnic groups, criticised the far-right Freedom Party for giving Austria a bad image abroad.
